format: Number-first cost confession, single take to camera

hook.visual: Founder holding one shoe, sole facing the lens, warehouse behind
hook.audio: It costs us ninety pounds more per pair to make this shoe, and we eat most of it.

script: It costs us ninety pounds more per pair to make this shoe, and we eat most of it.
Everyone asks why we don't just make them in Vietnam like everyone else.
The factory we use is in Portugal. Family owned, third generation, forty people.
They've made shoes for brands you'd recognise. They're not allowed to tell me which.
Here's the bit I can prove.
Industry return rate on running shoes is around eleven percent.
Ours is under three.
That gap is the ninety quid. We just moved it to the front of the process instead of the refund queue.
on_screen_text: Same money. Different end of the process.
caption: Would you rather we spent it on the shoe or the returns team?
share_reason: People who follow manufacturing and supply chain content send this to friends who bang on about where things are made
comment_trigger: The unnamed big brands made in the same factory. People will guess in the comments
why_views: A precise cost number spoken as a confession in the first second creates an immediate why, and the return rate pays it off before anyone can scroll.

format: Object as proof, result before the story

hook.visual: Beaten shoe dropped onto a table, camera pushes into the sole tread
hook.audio: This one's done twelve hundred kilometres.

script: This one's done twelve hundred kilometres.
That's the sole. Flip it over, that's the upper.
I'm not going to tell you it looks new, it doesn't. But it's still fine.
The reason isn't the rubber, it's the last.
The last is the foot shaped mould the shoe gets built on.
Most big brands run a handful of lasts across their entire range.
We scanned about four hundred runners' feet and built our own.
Wider toe box than you're used to. Nothing in the shoe is fighting your foot.
That's why this one's still here after twelve hundred kilometres.
on_screen_text: The 'last' = the mould the shoe is built on
Big brands: a handful of lasts for everything
caption: How far has your current pair actually gone?
share_reason: Runners send this to the friend who replaces their shoes every six months on principle
comment_trigger: Everyone posts their own mileage and argues about when shoes are 'dead'
why_views: A worn object on screen is instant evidence, and opening with the result means the explanation feels earned rather than pitched.

format: Stated hot take, audience split live

hook.visual: Founder mid shrug, close crop, no product visible yet
hook.audio: Forty percent of you are going to hate this, and that's fine.

script: Forty percent of you are going to hate this, and that's fine.
We don't do sales. Ever. No Black Friday, no twenty percent off code in a creator's bio.
The price is the price.
Here's why I can't move it.
The factory's in Portugal, family run, third generation, forty people.
It costs about ninety pounds more per pair than making them elsewhere, and we absorb most of that.
There's no margin sitting there waiting to be discounted off.
A sale would just mean I'd been overcharging you in November.
So, forty percent of you, off you go. Genuinely fine.
on_screen_text: No sales. No codes. No Black Friday.
A discount = you were overcharged before
caption: Never discounting: principled or just annoying?
share_reason: Sent between people who argue about pricing ethics and the discount treadmill, plus founders sending it to other founders
comment_trigger: A plainly stated hot take that splits the room, and the video literally invites the 40% to say so
why_views: Naming a percentage of the audience who will disagree in the first second makes both camps stay to find out which one they're in.

format: Two contradictory quotes on screen, silent build, reveal last

hook.visual: Black screen, white text appears, hands lacing a shoe underneath

script: First time anyone puts these on, they say the same thing.
It feels weird.
Second run, same person, different sentence.
It feels like nothing.
That second one is the whole goal.
Weird is just your foot noticing there's room in the toe box for once.
We built the mould from scans of about four hundred runners' feet instead of borrowing an old one.
You're not meant to feel a running shoe.
Which is why the first time, it feels weird.
on_screen_text: You're not meant to feel a shoe
caption: Weird for one run, then nothing. Worth it?
share_reason: Wide toe box people send this to friends who complain about cramped shoes and blackened toenails
comment_trigger: Direct disagreement about whether a shoe should feel like anything at all, plus people describing their own break-in experience
why_views: A quoted complaint as the opening line looks like criticism, so viewers stay to see how it gets resolved, and the last line loops back to the first.
